\subsection*{Data-Driven Clustering}

To assess the DDR partition structure and determine whether the drifting/non-drifting split is data-driven, we apply $k$-means clustering ($k \in \{2,3,4,5\}$) to the seven features in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space (Table~\ref{tab:clustering}).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{$k$-means clustering of 7 features in $(|\rho|, d)$ space.}
\label{tab:clustering}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{ccp{5.5cm}}
\toprule
$k$ & Silhouette & Clusters \\
\midrule
2 & \textbf{0.660} & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\min}$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} \\
3 & 0.532 & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\min}$\} \\
4 & 0.527 & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\max}$, tail\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\min}$\} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

The primary drifting/non-drifting split ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.660) is the strongest cluster structure.
At $k{=}3$, entropy min forms its own cluster rather than joining the near-stationary group because its pooled $|\rho|{=}0.40$ (driven by the gen-0/gen-1 boundary) places it far from other near-stationary features in $\rho$ space.
The 3/1/3 DDR partition resolves this by using the gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ Cohen's $d$ ($d{=}0.03$) to place entropy min in the near-stationary group, a domain-informed refinement that unsupervised clustering cannot recover from pooled statistics alone.
At $k{=}4$ (silhouette\,=\,0.571), entropy std separates from the near-stationary group, consistent with its intermediate DDR classification.

\paragraph{Exhaustive partition enumeration.}
To confirm that the three-vs-four split is optimal rather than incidental, we enumerate all $\binom{7}{3}{=}35$ possible ways to assign three features to a ``drifting'' group and the remaining four to ``non-drifting,'' computing the silhouette score for each partition in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space.
The observed DDR partition (\{entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio\}) achieves the highest silhouette (0.660), with a gap of 0.18 to the second-ranked split; 20 of 35 partitions produce negative silhouette scores.

\paragraph{Per-generator replication.}
To rule out the possibility that the pooled silhouette is an artifact of mixing heterogeneous generators, we repeat the $(|\rho|, d)$ clustering independently for each of the eight generators.
Every generator recovers the identical \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} vs.\ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\min}$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} partition, with silhouette scores ranging from 0.505 (Pythia-1B) to 0.760 (Mistral-7B-v0.3; mean\,=\,0.651).
No generator falls below the 0.50 moderate-structure threshold, confirming that the two-cluster structure is a per-generator property rather than a pooling artifact.

\subsection*{TOST Equivalence Bound Sensitivity}
\label{app:tost-sensitivity}

Table~\ref{tab:tost-sensitivity} shows the fraction of generators for which each feature passes the TOST equivalence test (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, $\alpha{=}0.05$) at three equivalence bounds $\varepsilon$.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{TOST equivalence pass rate across 8 generators at varying $\varepsilon$.}
\label{tab:tost-sensitivity}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
\textbf{DDR Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.15}$ & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.20}$ & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.25}$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
 & TTR & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 7/8 & 8/8 & 8/8 \\
 & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 6/8 & 6/8 & 6/8 \\
 & tail decay & 4/8 & 4/8 & 7/8 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

The partition is robust to the equivalence bound: drifting features reject equivalence at all $\varepsilon$ for all generators, while entropy min passes even at the stricter bound $\varepsilon{=}0.15$ (7/8 generators).
Tail decay is the most $\varepsilon$-sensitive near-stationary feature, passing 4/8 at $\varepsilon{=}0.20$ but 7/8 at $\varepsilon{=}0.25$; the four non-passing generators show $|d|{=}0.15$--$0.22$, still well below the drifting threshold ($d > 0.50$).
Entropy max is stable across all three bounds (6/8), with the two failures (Pythia-1B $d{=}0.21$, Pythia-2.8B $d{=}0.25$) reflecting same-family reference affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model.

\paragraph{Threshold sensitivity.}
To address concerns about the sensitivity of the drifting-boundary threshold,
we sweep $|d|$ from $0.10$ to $0.80$ in increments of $0.05$ and record the
resulting binary partition (drifting vs.\ stationary) along with the silhouette
score in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space.
Across the entire range, only \emph{three} distinct partitions emerge,
reflecting natural gaps between feature clusters rather than threshold artifacts.
The three-feature drifting set (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio)
is stable across $|d| \in [0.50,\, 0.75]$ with a silhouette of $0.660$---the
peak value in the sweep.
Including the intermediate feature entropy std ($d{=}0.49$) yields a
4/3 partition stable across $|d| \in [0.10,\, 0.45]$ (silhouette\,=\,0.451).
The partition used in our analysis corresponds to the peak-silhouette region,

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related}
3	
4	\subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}
5	\label{sec:related-detection}
6	
7	The detection literature spans statistical tests \cite{gltr,grover,release_strategies}, zero-shot scoring \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,dna_gpt}, surprisal diversity \cite{diveye}, spectral analysis of relative likelihood \cite{xu_spectrum_detection}, geometric invariants \cite{intrinsic_dim_detection}, and learned classifiers \cite{ghostbuster,feat_aug_transformer,reliable_detection,ld_score}; see \citet{wu_survey_2025} and \citet{jawahar_survey} for surveys.
8	RAID \cite{raid} benchmarks binary detection across generators and attacks; we extend the task from binary to ordinal depth estimation.
9	Several recent efforts move beyond the binary boundary (collaboration roles \cite{beyond_binary}, joint detection-attribution \cite{two_birds}, creator-editor modes \cite{beyond_final_actor}, multi-generator attribution \cite{semeval2024_task8}) but all taxonomize by \emph{source} or \emph{production mode}, not recursive generation \emph{depth}; repurposing their scores as depth predictors reveals high cross-generator variance (binary F1\,=\,0.54--0.71; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}) \cite{paraphrase_evades,detection_possibilities}.
10	Our contribution is orthogonal: ordinal depth classification \cite{gutierrez_ordinal_survey,diaz_soft_labels_ordinal,coral_ordinal,kasa_ordinality_nlp} as a task, and the finding that combining drifting and stationary features yields consistent cross-generator performance where individual detection scores show high variance \cite{uchendu_attribution,munir_looking_glass}.
11	
12	\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}
13	\label{sec:related-collapse}
14	
15	Self-consuming generative models progressively lose distributional coverage \cite{self_consuming_mad,curse_of_recursion,briesch_self_consuming,seddik_synthetic_data}, though data mixing mitigates collapse \cite{model_collapse_avoidable,strong_model_collapse}.
16	In particular, the autophagous loop formalized by \citet{self_consuming_mad} mirrors the recursive generation setup we construct at inference time, and \citet{dohmatob_tale_of_tails} provide a theoretical account showing that even minimal synthetic-data contamination alters scaling laws---predicting the distributional compression that DDR empirically decomposes into drifting and stationary components.
17	These studies address \emph{training-loop} degradation where parameter updates erode tail coverage; indeed, \citet{schaeffer_collapse_position} identify eight distinct definitions of ``collapse,'' most tied to retraining dynamics.
18	We examine \emph{inference chains} where parameters are fixed and only the input distribution evolves.
19	Two concurrent works address iterative generation from complementary perspectives: \citet{broken_telephone} study paraphrasing and translation chains, documenting progressive factuality degradation; \citet{markovian_chains} analyze Markovian convergence dynamics, bounding distinguishable depth to ${\sim}$3 classes; \citet{attractor_cycles} provide evidence for cyclic attractor states.
20	DDR differs along three dimensions: \emph{chain type}---non-paraphrastic continuation, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal; \emph{analysis lens}---a location/shape decomposition that identifies what is preserved, not just what converges; and \emph{downstream utility}---shape stability provides a cross-generator reference enabling ordinal classification without per-generator calibration.
21	All three approaches observe qualitative saturation within ${\sim}$3--5 iterations despite different chain types and metrics (a detailed finding-level comparison appears in Appendix~\ref{app:iterative-comparison}).
22	
23	\subsection{Vocabulary Diversity and Stylometry}
24	\label{sec:related-diversity}
25	
26	Declining lexical diversity in LLM text is documented in both training \cite{curious_decline} and deployment settings \cite{writing_diversity}; MAUVE \cite{mauve} provides a divergence-based metric for quantifying this distributional gap.
27	\citeauthor{curious_decline}'s finding that recursive training progressively impoverishes vocabulary aligns with the monotonic decline of TTR and hapax ratio we observe across generation depths; these surface features constitute the drifting component of DDR.
28	More broadly, our surface features are classical stylometric measures \cite{stamatatos_survey,koppel_authorship}; we repurpose them from generator identity \cite{uchendu_attribution} to the depth dimension, where their monotonic decline under top-$p$ sampling \cite{nucleus_sampling,welleck_unlikelihood} provides a complementary signal to reference-model statistics.
29	
30	\paragraph{Data quality and provenance.}
31	Scalable data curation relies on quality signals \cite{dsir,qurating,ccnet}; generation depth offers a complementary provenance axis.
32	Proactive watermarking \cite{watermark_llm,synthid_text,aaronson_watermark} embeds identifiable patterns at generation time but requires generator cooperation and degrades across multi-step chains \cite{chainwash}; our approach is entirely post-hoc, requiring no modification to the generation process and remaining applicable when watermarking is absent or has washed out.
33	Our NLL-based analysis connects to \citet{min_k_percent} (probability-tail membership inference) but extends from binary membership to full distributional decomposition for ordinal depth.
34	\citet{koike_mia_detection} formalize this connection from the opposite direction, showing that detection scores implicitly perform membership inference, underscoring the shared statistical basis of detection and provenance.

\paragraph{Partition stability across $\varepsilon$ thresholds.}
\label{app:epsilon-sweep}

The DDR partition classifies features as non-stationary ($d \geq \varepsilon$) or stationary ($d < \varepsilon$) based on pooled Cohen's $d$ (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
Table~\ref{tab:epsilon-sweep} reports the critical $\varepsilon$ at which each feature's classification changes; the three drifting and three near-stationary features maintain their classification for all $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Partition stability under varying $\varepsilon$. Critical threshold: the $\varepsilon$ above which a feature is reclassified as stationary. The drifting/near-stationary split is invariant for $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$; only entropy std ($d{=}0.55$) changes at $\varepsilon > 0.55$.}
\label{tab:epsilon-sweep}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
\textbf{DDR Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Pooled $d$} & \textbf{Stationary at $\varepsilon >$} \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 1.17 & 1.17 \\
 & TTR & 0.88 & 0.88 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0.76 & 0.76 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0.55 & 0.55 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 0.08 & 0.08 \\
 & tail decay & 0.08 & 0.08 \\
 & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 0.016 & 0.016 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\noindent The 3/1/3 partition is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$: the three drifting features remain non-stationary at all $\varepsilon < 0.76$, the three near-stationary features remain stationary at all $\varepsilon > 0.08$, and only entropy std changes classification (becoming stationary at $\varepsilon > 0.55$), confirming it as the sole threshold-sensitive feature.
The minimum gap between adjacent zone boundaries ($d_{\text{hapax}} - d_{\sigma_H} = 0.21$) exceeds typical effect-size estimation uncertainty, providing a margin against sampling noise.

\subsection*{Holdout Generator Split Validation}
\label{app:holdout-split}

To confirm the DDR partition is not an artifact of the specific generator pool, we split the eight generators into disjoint selection (4) and validation (4) sets, compute per-subset pooled $(|\rho|, d)$, and check whether all seven features receive the same zone assignment in both subsets.
We evaluate two complementary splits to avoid dependence on a single partition:
Split~A selects \{Pythia-2.8B, Qwen3-1.7B, OLMo, Mistral\} (validation: Pythia-1B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B, Llama);
Split~B selects \{Pythia-1B, Qwen3-0.6B, OLMo, Mistral\} (validation: Pythia-2.8B, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, Llama).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Holdout split validation of the DDR partition. Selection (sel) and validation (val) $|\rho|$ and $d$ for two disjoint 4/4 generator splits. Zone assignment is identical across all four subsets for every feature.}
\label{tab:holdout-split}

\begin{tabular}{llcccccc}
\toprule
& & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Split A}} & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Split B}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){3-5} \cmidrule(lr){6-8}
\textbf{Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & sel $|\rho|$ & val $|\rho|$ & $\Delta|\rho|$ & sel $|\rho|$ & val $|\rho|$ & $\Delta|\rho|$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 0.60 & 0.58 & 0.02 & 0.60 & 0.58 & 0.02 \\
 & TTR & 0.61 & 0.59 & 0.02 & 0.60 & 0.59 & 0.01 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0.62 & 0.60 & 0.02 & 0.62 & 0.61 & 0.01 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0.19 & 0.21 & 0.02 & 0.22 & 0.17 & 0.05 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 0.39 & 0.36 & 0.03 & 0.38 & 0.37 & 0.01 \\
 & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 0.05 & 0.05 & 0.00 & 0.04 & 0.06 & 0.02 \\
 & tail decay & 0.10 & 0.08 & 0.02 & 0.11 & 0.07 & 0.04 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

Under simple joint $(|\rho|, d)$ thresholds, both splits produce a 3/2/2 partition: entropy min is classified as a second intermediate feature due to its elevated pooled $|\rho|$ (0.36--0.39).
However, entropy min's binary (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) $d$ values are uniformly below 0.06 across all four split${\times}$subset combinations, consistent with near-stationarity on the task-relevant metric; its pooled $|\rho|$ reflects change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary rather than sustained drift.
Five of seven features are unambiguously classified under any reasonable criterion; entropy min's boundary status is resolved by the binary-task $d$ criterion.

Selection and validation subsets produce identical partitions in both splits (Table~\ref{tab:holdout-split}; Figure~\ref{fig:holdout-scatter}).
The maximum $\Delta|\rho|$ between selection and validation is 0.05 (entropy std, Split~B), and the minimum gap between adjacent zones remains $>$0.15 in all subsets.

\begin{figure}[H]

\caption{Holdout split validation in $(|\rho|, d)$ space. Filled markers: selection set; hollow: validation set. Zone assignments are identical across subsets; selection/validation pairs cluster tightly for all features.}
\label{fig:holdout-scatter}
\end{figure}

\subsection*{Heteroscedasticity Sensitivity}
\label{app:heteroscedasticity}

Levene tests reject equal variance between gen-1 and gen-2+ for drifting features ($p < 10^{-10}$; variance ratios 1.86--2.21).
To verify that the DDR partition is robust to this heteroscedasticity, we supplement pooled Cohen's $d$ with Glass's $\Delta$ (using the gen-1 standard deviation as denominator) and Cliff's $\delta$ (a non-parametric ordinal effect size; Table~\ref{tab:effect-sizes}).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Effect size comparison (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, $N$\,=\,29{,}095). Glass's $\Delta$ uses the gen-1 SD as denominator; Cliff's $\delta$ thresholds follow Romano et al.\ (2006): $|\delta| < 0.147$ negligible, $< 0.33$ small, $< 0.474$ medium, otherwise large.}
\label{tab:effect-sizes}
\begin{tabular}{llrrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & \textbf{$|d|$} & \textbf{$|\Delta|$} & \textbf{$|\delta|$} \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & ent.\ mean & 1.054 & 1.410 & 0.587 \\
 & TTR & 0.814 & 1.116 & 0.510 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0.735 & 0.936 & 0.528 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & ent.\ std & 0.457 & 0.605 & 0.295 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & tail decay & 0.087 & 0.099 & 0.072 \\
 & ent.\ max & 0.062 & 0.065 & 0.021 \\
 & ent.\ min & 0.016 & 0.015 & 0.354$^{\dagger}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\noindent Effect sizes in Table~\ref{tab:effect-sizes} are computed on the binary task (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+); the main text (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) reports 3-class pooled $d$ values (e.g., hapax ratio $d{=}0.76$), which are slightly larger because the gen-0/gen-1 contrast contributes additional separation.
Glass's $\Delta$ amplifies drifting effects (1.41 vs.\ 1.05 for entropy mean) because gen-2+ variance exceeds gen-1 variance (ratio 2.08), making the pooled Cohen's $d$ conservative.
Near-stationary features remain negligible under both parametric metrics ($|\Delta| \leq 0.099$).
The minimum drifting-to-maximum-near-stationary gap is $9.5\times$ under Glass's $\Delta$ (0.936\,/\,0.099); heteroscedasticity does not erode the partition.
Cliff's $\delta$ classifies all drifting features as ``large'' ($|\delta| > 0.474$) and entropy std as ``small'' ($|\delta|{=}0.295$), consistent with the parametric partition.

\noindent $^{\dagger}$Entropy min's elevated Cliff's $\delta$ (0.354, ``medium'') reflects distributional shape asymmetry between gen-1 and gen-2+ that rank-based statistics detect but location measures do not (Cohen's $d{=}0.016$, Glass's $\Delta{=}0.015$).
This is consistent with its documented boundary status (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}): the gen-0/gen-1 transition produces rank-order shifts that persist into deeper generations without affecting the mean.

We expect 8-generator training to further improve given additional diversity; the comparison direction is preserved.}

24	\paragraph{Results.}
25	QLoRA achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.905 ($\pm$0.003) under 6-generator LOGO, a +11.6\,pp improvement over the same-subset XGBoost baseline (0.789).
26	On 5-class evaluation, QLoRA reaches F1\,=\,0.583 ($\pm$0.010) vs.\ 0.501 for XGBoost (+8.2\,pp), with the largest gains at gen-1 (0.796 vs.\ 0.634) and gen-2 (0.413 vs.\ 0.268).

32	\paragraph{Implications.}

% Abstract — Depth Profiling of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
As LLM outputs re-enter training corpora and seed further generation, understanding how recursive generation reshapes text distributions becomes important for data provenance and corpus curation---yet existing detectors answer only the binary human-or-machine question, ignoring \emph{generation depth}: we introduce \emph{depth profiling} to address this gap.
We decompose distributional drift under recursive generation into location and shape components, revealing an asymmetry we term \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): across eight base-model generators from five families, NLL location features drift monotonically with depth ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) while three shape features remain near-stationary ($d < 0.10$), with entropy std intermediate ($d{=}0.55$).
Prior work documents \emph{what converges}; the central finding here is \emph{what is approximately preserved}: shape invariance provides a cross-generator reference that enables coarse ordinal depth classification (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) without per-generator calibration, achieving leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) under leave-one-generator-out evaluation; an end-to-end classifier reaches 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 (6-gen LOGO; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}).
Instruction tuning compresses DDR, bounding current applicability to base models.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	An estimated 7--17\% of recent scientific publications already contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}. As these outputs re-enter training corpora \cite{dolma,fineweb} and seed further generation, text accumulates at varying \emph{generation depths}; each successive cycle reshapes distributional properties in ways that matter for data provenance, corpus auditing, and contamination monitoring in base-model pretraining corpora \cite{ccnet,dsir} as well as model collapse analysis \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}. Understanding \emph{how} recursive generation alters text distributions---and which properties change versus which are preserved---is therefore a prerequisite for principled corpus curation, yet current methods address only binary human-or-machine detection \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score}.
5	Base models provide the cleanest substrate to isolate depth effects from alignment-induced changes.
6	We find that recursive generation produces a decomposable depth profile: distributional \emph{location} drifts with depth while \emph{shape} remains stable across generators, an asymmetry sufficient for cross-generator depth prediction.
7	
8	Distributional compression under recursive generation is well-documented \cite{curious_decline,broken_telephone,markovian_chains}, yet existing analyses characterize \emph{that} and \emph{why} convergence occurs without decomposing what drifts from what is preserved.
9	We introduce \emph{depth profiling} (Figure~\ref{fig:framework}), classifying text by ordinal generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+), and decompose this compression into structurally distinct components: across eight base-model generators spanning five architectural families (0.6B--8B), the NLL distribution's central tendency (mean entropy (reference-model NLL), lexical diversity) drifts monotonically with depth while its shape (entropy extremes, tail structure) remains an order of magnitude more stable ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$ vs.\ $d < 0.10$ for three near-stationary features; entropy std is intermediate ($d{=}0.55$); boundary features show additional nuance; convergent effect-size measures confirm this partition).
10	We term this location/shape asymmetry the \emph{differential depth response} (DDR; Figure~\ref{fig:ddr-trajectory}), an empirical regularity of base-model autoregressive generation that is mechanistically distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion}, which erodes tail coverage via weight updates; DDR instead analyzes fixed-parameter inference chains.
11	The stationary shape component provides the cross-generator reference needed for depth prediction without per-generator calibration.
12	
13	\begin{figure*}[t!]
14	\centering
15	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig2_framework.pdf}
16	\caption{Depth profiling framework. (a)~Recursive generation chain: a human-written seed (gen-0) is iteratively fed through a generator $G$ to produce text at successive depths; eight base-model LLMs across five families (0.6B--8B) serve as generators. (b)~Feature extraction: each text is scored by a fixed reference model (Pythia-410M), yielding five NLL statistics and two surface diversity measures (seven DDR features total). (c)~Leave-One-Generator-Out evaluation: XGBoost classifies each text into gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ with one generator held out per fold.}
17	\label{fig:framework}
18	\end{figure*}
19	We focus on base (pretrained) models; instruction tuning degrades depth signal (Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}).
20	
21	As a proof of concept, a lightweight 7-feature ensemble informed by DDR achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, matching multi-detector ensembles at ${\sim}2.4\times$ lower cost; an end-to-end QLoRA classifier reaches 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 (6-gen LOGO; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming that the depth signal extends well beyond handcrafted features.
22	
23	Our contributions:
24	\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
25	    \item \textbf{Empirical decomposition (DDR).} Across eight generators from five families, we decompose inference-chain drift into a location component that shifts monotonically ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) and a shape component that remains near-stationary ($d < 0.10$ for three near-stationary features). Where prior work documents \emph{what converges} \cite{curious_decline,markovian_chains}, DDR identifies \emph{what is approximately preserved} and enables depth detection without per-generator calibration. DDR is a descriptive empirical finding; the classification value lies in this decomposition rather than the classifier itself.
26	    \item \textbf{Task formulation and evaluation suite.} We define generation depth classification as an ordinal prediction task and construct a controlled dataset of 37K texts from eight generators across five families (0.6B--8B; exploratory evidence extends to 14B, Appendix~\ref{app:9gen-scale}), with leave-one-generator-out cross-validation as the primary evaluation protocol.
27	    \item \textbf{Scope characterization.} Systematic evaluation across temperature, prompt type, instruction tuning, model scale, domain transfer, and perturbation robustness maps the operational envelope of depth profiling.
28	\end{enumerate}

% Abstract — Depth Profiling of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
As LLM outputs re-enter training corpora and seed further generation, understanding how recursive generation reshapes text distributions becomes important for data provenance and corpus curation---yet existing detectors answer only the binary human-or-machine question, ignoring \emph{generation depth}: we introduce \emph{depth profiling} to address this gap.

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	An estimated 7--17\% of recent scientific publications already contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}. As these outputs re-enter training corpora \cite{dolma,fineweb} and seed further generation, text accumulates at varying \emph{generation depths}; each successive cycle reshapes distributional properties in ways that matter for data provenance, corpus auditing, and contamination monitoring in base-model pretraining corpora \cite{ccnet,dsir} as well as model collapse analysis \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}. Understanding \emph{how} recursive generation alters text distributions---and which properties change versus which are preserved---is therefore a prerequisite for principled corpus curation, yet current methods address only binary human-or-machine detection \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score}.
5	Base models provide the cleanest substrate to isolate depth effects from alignment-induced changes.
6	We find that recursive generation produces a decomposable depth profile: distributional \emph{location} drifts with depth while \emph{shape} remains stable across generators, an asymmetry sufficient for cross-generator depth prediction.
7	
8	Distributional compression under recursive generation is well-documented \cite{curious_decline,broken_telephone,markovian_chains}, yet existing analyses characterize \emph{that} and \emph{why} convergence occurs without decomposing what drifts from what is preserved.
9	We introduce \emph{depth profiling} (coarse ordinal classification into gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+; Figure~\ref{fig:framework}), and decompose this compression into structurally distinct components: across eight base-model generators spanning five architectural families (0.6B--8B), the NLL distribution's central tendency (mean entropy (reference-model NLL), lexical diversity) drifts monotonically with depth while its shape (entropy extremes, tail structure) remains an order of magnitude more stable ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$ vs.\ $d < 0.10$ for three near-stationary features; entropy std is intermediate ($d{=}0.55$); boundary features show additional nuance; convergent effect-size measures confirm this partition).
10	We term this location/shape asymmetry the \emph{differential depth response} (DDR; Figure~\ref{fig:ddr-trajectory}), an empirical regularity of base-model autoregressive generation that is mechanistically distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion}, which erodes tail coverage via weight updates; DDR instead analyzes fixed-parameter inference chains.
11	The stationary shape component complements location drift for depth prediction without per-generator calibration.
12	
13	\begin{figure*}[t!]
14	\centering
15	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig2_framework.pdf}
16	\caption{Depth profiling framework. (a)~Recursive generation chain: a human-written seed (gen-0) is iteratively fed through a generator $G$ to produce text at successive depths; eight base-model LLMs across five families (0.6B--8B) serve as generators. (b)~Feature extraction: each text is scored by a fixed reference model (Pythia-410M), yielding five NLL statistics and two surface diversity measures (seven DDR features total). (c)~Leave-One-Generator-Out evaluation: XGBoost classifies each text into gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ with one generator held out per fold.}
17	\label{fig:framework}
18	\end{figure*}
19	We focus on base (pretrained) models; instruction tuning degrades depth signal (Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}).
20	
21	As a proof of concept, a lightweight 7-feature ensemble informed by DDR achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, matching multi-detector ensembles at ${\sim}2.4\times$ lower cost; an end-to-end QLoRA classifier reaches 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 (6-gen LOGO; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming that the depth signal extends well beyond handcrafted features.
22	
23	Our contributions:
24	\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
25	    \item \textbf{Empirical decomposition (DDR).} Across eight generators from five families, we decompose inference-chain drift into three response zones: drifting ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$), intermediate ($d{=}0.55$), and near-stationary ($d < 0.10$). Where prior work documents \emph{what converges} \cite{curious_decline,markovian_chains}, DDR identifies \emph{what is approximately preserved}, an empirical regularity with analytical utility for depth classification without per-generator calibration. DDR is a descriptive empirical finding; the classification value lies in this decomposition rather than the classifier itself.
26	    \item \textbf{Task formulation and evaluation suite.} We define generation depth classification as an ordinal prediction task and construct a controlled dataset of 37K texts from eight generators across five families (0.6B--8B; exploratory evidence extends to 14B, Appendix~\ref{app:9gen-scale}), with leave-one-generator-out cross-validation as the primary evaluation protocol.
27	    \item \textbf{Scope characterization.} Systematic evaluation across temperature, prompt type, instruction tuning, model scale, domain transfer, and perturbation robustness maps the operational envelope of depth profiling.
28	\end{enumerate}
29

1	\vspace{-1mm}
2	\section*{Limitations}
3	\label{sec:limitations}
4	\vspace{-1mm}
5	
6	\looseness=-1 All eight generators are base (pretrained) models with $\leq$8.2B parameters; exploratory evidence at 14B (Appendix~\ref{app:9gen-scale}) suggests persistence but is based on a single model, and behavior at larger scales remains unverified.
7	Instruction-tuned variants show substantially degraded depth signal (within-model 3-class F1: Llama 0.544, OLMo 0.575, Qwen 0.732; LOGO binary F1\,=\,0.487; Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}), and Gemma-2-2B exhibits near-zero gen-1 F1 (binary F1\,=\,0.440; gen-1 nearly undetectable) due to tokenizer and attention differences (Appendix~\ref{app:9gen-scale}).
8	We attribute this degradation to RLHF and instruction tuning, which reshape the token-level NLL distribution---flattening entropy peaks and compressing lexical diversity variation---thereby attenuating the DDR signal that depth classification relies on.
9	An end-to-end QLoRA classifier partially recovers depth discrimination on instruct-generated text (F1\,=\,0.89--0.91; Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}), suggesting that the underlying depth signal is compressed rather than eliminated; the handcrafted features are too coarse to capture it in the instruct regime.
10	The current method is therefore most applicable to base-model-generated text, with primary use cases in pretraining data contamination detection, model collapse monitoring, and synthetic data provenance---settings where base models are the dominant source of recursive generation.
11	Extending depth profiling to instruction-tuned models remains open; instruct-specific feature engineering (e.g., instruction-following markers, response-format statistics) or adapter-based domain adaptation may recover the compressed signal.
12	
13	The evaluation assumes a fixed decoding regime (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$) with English Wikipedia seeds and an English-centric reference model (Pythia-410M); cross-temperature transfer degrades at mismatched settings (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}). 14	
15	Depth resolution is bounded at three classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+); finer-grained 5-class classification yields F1\,$\approx$\,0.50 with deeper depths mutually indistinguishable (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}).

\begin{abstract}

lines: We find that recursive generation produces a decomposable depth profile: distributional \emph{location} drifts with depth while \emph{shape} remains stable across generators, an asymmetry sufficient for cross-generator depth prediction.

Distributional compression under recursive generation is well-documented \cite{curious_decline,broken_telephone,markovian_chains}, yet existing analyses characterize \emph{that} and \emph{why} convergence occurs without decomposing what drifts from what is preserved.

-We introduce \emph{depth profiling} (coarse ordinal classification into gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+; Figure~\ref{fig:framework}), and decompose this compression into structurally distinct components: across eight base-model generators spanning five architectural families (0.6B--8B), the NLL distribution's central tendency (mean entropy (reference-model NLL), lexical diversity) drifts monotonically with depth while its shape (entropy extremes, tail structure) remains an order of magnitude more stable ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$ vs.\ $d < 0.10$ for three near-stationary features; entropy std is intermediate ($d{=}0.55$); boundary features show additional nuance; convergent effect-size measures confirm this partition).

+We introduce \emph{depth profiling} (coarse ordinal classification into gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+; Figure~\ref{fig:framework}), and decompose this compression into structurally distinct components: across eight base-model generators spanning five architectural families (0.6B--8B), the NLL distribution's central tendency (mean entropy (reference-model NLL), lexical diversity) drifts monotonically with depth while its shape (entropy extremes, tail structure) remains an order of magnitude more stable (effect size $d{=}0.76$--$1.17$ vs.\ $d < 0.10$ for three near-stationary features; entropy std is intermediate ($d{=}0.55$); boundary features show additional nuance; convergent effect-size measures confirm this partition).

We term this location/shape asymmetry the \emph{differential depth response} (DDR; Figure~\ref{fig:ddr-trajectory}), an empirical regularity of base-model autoregressive generation that is mechanistically distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion}, which erodes tail coverage via weight updates; DDR instead analyzes fixed-parameter inference chains.
The stationary shape component complements location drift for depth prediction without per-generator calibration.
